claim: Running header 'L I B E R' rendered as 'BOOK THREE' (page 162 belongs to Book III)
evidence: Book III opens at scan page 154 ('ARTIS GYMNASTICAE LIBER TERTIVS ... Cap. 1') and closes at scan page 210 ('Explicit Liber Tertius'); scan page 184 (p. 162) falls inside it, and odd-page headers in this range read 'TERTIVS'.

claim: Note identifies the editor who judges the Hymn to Artemis 'a worthless piece of work' as Gemoll
evidence: This book is 'Die homerischen Hymnen, herausgegeben und erläutert von Albert Gemoll' (Leipzig: Teubner, 1886), so the commentary on the page is Gemoll's own.

claim: Meta calls the harsh cold 'the third cause' of leaf loss
evidence: The previous page lists three causes ('tres suelen ser las causas'): the sun's absence in winter, dryness, and summer heat. On this page the cold is added 'por vltima causa', so it is an additional fourth, final cause.
correction: The cold is a fourth cause, added at the end ('as a final cause'). The third cause is summer heat.

claim: Running header 'ON ABSTINENCE FROM' expanded to 'ON ABSTINENCE FROM [ANIMAL FOOD.—BOOK II.]'
evidence: In Taylor's translation the passages on this page (sections 13–15, including the Thessalian who sacrificed oxen with gilt horns to the Pythian god) are in Book II of 'On Abstinence from Animal Food'.

claim: 'that which is useless to them' glossed as 'useless to the plants ... such as their fruit'
evidence: Section 13 reads 'For bees collect their honey from plants; but we carefully attend to them... But that which is useless to them, and beneficial to us, will be the reward...': 'them' means the bees, and the reward is their surplus honey.
correction: 'Useless to them' means useless to the bees: the surplus honey they produce, not the plants' fruit.

claim: 'Pythian deity' identified as Apollo at the oracle of Delphi
evidence: The same passage continues 'Apollo said, that the offering of Hermioneus was more gratifying to him'.

claim: Running header '奇器圖說' rendered as 'Wonderful Machines of the Far West' (identifies the work as 遠西奇器圖說)
evidence: The work is 遠西奇器圖說錄最, 'Diagrams and Explanations of the Wonderful Machines of the Far West' (Schreck and Wang Zheng, 1627), so the identification is right. The page header itself is only the abbreviated 奇器圖說 and does not include 遠西 ('of the Far West').
correction: Not wrong. A literal rendering of the header would be 'Diagrams and Explanations of Wonderful Machines'.

claim: Dikpalas: Indra rules the East and Yama rules the South
evidence: Among the Ashta-Dikpalas, Indra is guardian of the East and Yama of the South.

claim: Meta names the work 'Lamp of Inquiry' (Prashna Deepak)
evidence: The Source Library catalogue title of this manuscript is 'Prashna Deepakam'; praśna means 'question' and dīpaka 'lamp'. Only the catalogue identification is confirmed; the page itself carries no title.

claim: Abbreviation 鉉 expanded as 'Genpuku-ji'
evidence: The article's locality key (p. 408) has no 鉉. It lists （鉛）鉛山 (Kanayama, Nishimuro district), so 鉉 is almost certainly an OCR misreading of 鉛. Genpuku-ji is not in the key.
correction: 鉛 (OCR 鉉) = Kanayama (鉛山), Nishimuro district

claim: Abbreviation 札 expanded as 'Sapporo'
evidence: The key on p. 407 reads '(札)札幌地方' (Sapporo district; specimens sent by Itō Seiya).

claim: Abbreviation 瀬 expanded as 'Setokanayama'
evidence: The key gives '（瀨）瀨戸' (Seto) and a separate '（鉛）鉛山' (Kanayama). The note merges the two localities.
correction: 瀬 = Seto (瀨戸), Nishimuro district

claim: Abbreviation 安 expanded as 'Anto' / 'Anto Peak'
evidence: The key gives '（安）二川村安堵峯' glossed アンドガミネ, i.e. Andogamine (Ando Peak) in Futagawa village. The place is right but the reading is 'Ando', not 'Anto'.
correction: Andogamine (安堵峯), Futagawa village

claim: Abbreviation 川 expanded as 'Kawakami'
evidence: The key gives '（川）日高郡川又', which is Kawamata in Hidaka district.
correction: Kawamata (川又), Hidaka district

claim: Abbreviation 坂 expanded as 'Sakayasu'
evidence: The key gives '（坂）同村坂泰' (坂泰 in Futagawa village) with no kana gloss, so the reading 'Sakayasu' cannot be confirmed from the page.

claim: Abbreviation 西 expanded as 'Nishimuro'
evidence: The key gives '（西）西ノ谷村' glossed ニシノダニ: Nishinotani village, one locality inside Nishimuro district, not the district itself.
correction: Nishinotani village (西ノ谷村)

claim: Abbreviation 稻 expanded as 'Inami'
evidence: The key gives '（稻）稻成' glossed イナリ, i.e. Inari.
correction: Inari (稻成), Nishimuro district

claim: Abbreviation 糸 expanded as 'Ito'
evidence: The key gives '（糸）糸田', i.e. Itoda.
correction: Itoda (糸田)

claim: Abbreviation 東 expanded as 'Higashimuro'
evidence: The key on p. 407 gives '(東)東京、草野博士所集': Tokyo, specimens collected by Dr Kusano.
correction: Tokyo (東京), Dr Kusano's collections

claim: Abbreviations 田, 和, 那, 天 expanded as Tanabe, Wakayama, Nachi, Tenma
evidence: The key gives （田）田邊町, （和）和歌山市, （那）那智山 and （天）天滿.

claim: Body: 'Extremely abundant at Anto Peak and Sakayasu in America' (米 read as the location of the peaks)
evidence: The introduction says foreign countries are listed after the localities. 米 (USA) is a separate entry, and Andogamine and 坂泰 are villages in Kii, Japan, not in America.
correction: 'Also America (USA). Extremely abundant at Andogamine and 坂泰.'

claim: Proclus was a 4th-century Neoplatonist who headed the Platonic school at Alexandria
evidence: Proclus lived 412–485 CE (5th century) and succeeded Syrianus as head of the Platonic Academy in Athens (c. 437).
correction: 5th-century (412–485) Neoplatonist, head of the Platonic Academy at Athens

claim: 浮園 (Buyuan) is the author's nickname
evidence: Catalogue record gives the author as Ch'oe Hyang-wŏn with ho Songae (松厓, from the title); no source found linking the sobriquet 浮園 to him, and the preface only says 浮園 brought and showed the collection.

claim: 浮園 is Ch'oe Hyang-wŏn
evidence: The page names only 浮園; no reference work found (web search for Songae sich'o / Ch'oe Hyang-wŏn returned nothing) identifying 浮園 with the catalogued author.

claim: 庚子 year = likely 1840
evidence: Book is catalogued 'ca. 1800', author described as late-18th-century; 庚子 could equally be 1780 or 1840 and nothing on the page fixes the cycle.
correction: A 庚子 year near the book's ca. 1800 date could be 1780 or 1840; the page does not decide.

claim: Summary/keywords: the preface praises the author Ch'oe Hyang-wŏn
evidence: The preface praises 浮園; whether 浮園 is the catalogued author Ch'oe Hyang-wŏn is not established by the page or any source found.

claim: Heading: Treatise on Armament Technology (Wubei zhi), Volume 139
evidence: The Zhanduzai section (93 juan) occupies juan 148-240 (Wikisource TOC: 占度載九十三卷), so juan 139 is outside it; this book's own OCR on pp. 4 and 22 reads 武備志卷一百四十九 占度載 占日一 for this run of pages (p. 15's 一百三十九 is the outlier the heading copied).
correction: Juan 149 (卷一百四十九), Zhanduzai, Divination of the Sun 1

claim: Heading: Divination of the Sun (Part II)
evidence: Running heads on pp. 2 and 22 of this book read 占日一 (Sun, part 1); 占日二 only begins at p. 37 (卷一百五十 占三 占日二), so p. 17 is in part I.
correction: Divination of the Sun (Part I) — 占日一

claim: Heading: Page 9 (folio number)
evidence: This page's OCR carries no folio number; p. 15 shows folio 七 and p. 22 shows 十一, which neither confirms nor rules out 九 for p. 17.

claim: Fragment '...ent.' continuing text from the previous page
evidence: The page's source begins with a fresh sentence 日有黃直…, and the previous page's translation ends a complete sentence ('will kill the enemy general.'), so there is no carried-over fragment.
correction: Delete the fragment.

claim: An illustration on this page depicts the hierarchy of the guru lineages within the central triangle of the Sri Chakra
evidence: The page's OCR is page-type 'text': Sanskrit verses 109-111 with commentary, Hindi translation and footnotes, with no image or diagram recorded; the note invents an illustration.
correction: No illustration on this page; remove the note.

claim: Higgins's 'ais' is Hebrew אִישׁ
evidence: Higgins glosses 'asr, ais' as 'incantator ignis' (enchanter of FIRE), so 'ais' stands for fire (אֵשׁ, esh); אִישׁ (ish) means 'man' (Wiktionary), and the source prints no Hebrew for 'ais'.
correction: If Hebrew is supplied it should be אֵשׁ (fire); better to leave 'ais' unglossed as Higgins did.

claim: The Samaritan text renders hbr hbr as asr, asr (אָסַר אָסַר)
evidence: The source reads 'by אָסַר asr, asr'; the translation only repeats the Hebrew to match the doubled transliteration, which is faithful to Higgins's statement.

claim: The page follows the earthquake and the 'Gloria' sung by the souls on the terrace of Avarice (end of Purgatorio XX)
evidence: Wikipedia: on the fifth terrace (avarice and prodigality) 'there is a sudden earthquake accompanied by the shouting of Gloria in excelsis Deo', and this page opens Canto XXI.

claim: The new companion is the poet Statius, who will explain these phenomena
evidence: Wikipedia: 'Statius reveals the earthquake's cause'; the canto rubric on the page also says they learn the cause of the shaking from a soul who turns out to be a poet.

claim: The commentator likely means Luke 24 (Emmaus), not Luke 23
evidence: The Emmaus appearance is in Luke 24:13-35.

claim: Geronimo surrendered to General George Custer in 1886
evidence: Geronimo surrendered on 4 September 1886 at Skeleton Canyon to Gen. Nelson A. Miles; Custer had died at the Little Bighorn in 1876. The year is right but the general is wrong.
correction: He surrendered to General Nelson A. Miles (Skeleton Canyon, 4 September 1886).

claim: One of the two women in the woodcut (white robe, making the beds) represents Chastity
evidence: On the next page the lady with the gauntlets who keeps the dormitory names herself: 'You may call me Chastity… I keep this dormitory cleanly'. On this page she is the one in the white rochet spreading the white sheets.

claim: Voluntary Poverty is the figure holding the staff
evidence: In the poem, the lady with the staff and gauntlets is the bed-maker (Chastity); Voluntary Poverty wears only the gambeson. The page's image description does give the staff to the gambeson-wearer, so text and woodcut description disagree.
correction: By the text, the staff belongs to Chastity; Poverty wears the gambeson.

claim: The page covers comic poets and historical figures (Nicostratus, Nicon)
evidence: The page runs νιφοσιβεῖς to νομοθέται (header); there is no entry for Nicostratus, Nicon or any comic poet.
correction: Entries niphosibeis to nomothetai: noema, notheia, nomades (Scythians), nomarchai, Numa, nomisma, nomographoi (decemvirs, Appius and Verginia), nomothetai (Moses, Christ).

claim: The page defines terms related to the letter N and the early Greek alphabet
evidence: The entries are N-words (νι–νο), but nothing on the page concerns the early Greek alphabet.
correction: Drop 'early Greek alphabet'.

claim: Keywords Nicostratus, Nicophon, Nicon
evidence: None of these names appears in the source text, which lies alphabetically after νικ- (header νιφοσιβεῖς — νομοθέται).
correction: Remove; the other keywords (Scythians, nomisma, Decemviri, Moses, Jesus Christ) are on the page.

claim: Judge 'McCormick' was 'often known as McComas' (i.e. McCormick is his name, McComas an alias)
evidence: The victim was Judge Hamilton C. McComas, killed with his wife by Chato's Chiricahua raiders on 28 March 1883 between Silver City and Lordsburg; his son Charley was taken. The identification with McComas is right, but 'McCormick' is Barrett's misprint (the pencil margin note corrects it), not a name he was known by.
correction: Judge Hamilton C. McComas; 'McCormick' is the book's error. Suggested wording: 'McCormick [recte McComas]'. The book's date of 1884 is also wrong: the raid was in 1883.

claim: Summary/keywords identify the episode as the 'McComas/McCormick incident'
evidence: This page describes the 1883 McComas massacre on the Silver City–Lordsburg road, and the margin annotation reads 'McComas'.

claim: The Oxford Slouch is the 'Old Serpent' character, 'Oxford Slouch' being his nickname
evidence: Book p.73 (scan page 77): 'the Serpent will be the Old Serpent, and also the Oxford Slouch'. Page 19 says he was called the 'Oxford Slouch' because of his manner of walking.

claim: The rites for Jupiter were concluded on the previous page
evidence: The previous page (scan page 8) ends 'इति गुरुन्यास समाप्तः' and invokes 'नमामि वृहस्पतिम्', i.e. the Jupiter (Guru/Brihaspati) nyāsa ends there.

claim: Cornerus is Johannes Cornerus, the official named on the previous page, who could not attend because of illness
evidence: The previous page names 'D. JOHANNES CORNERUS, S. Theol. Doctor ... Vice-Cancellarius ... qui adversâ jam valetudine morbum curat sonticum', meaning he is kept away by serious illness.

claim: Meta: the speaker stands in for the high-ranking official Johannes Cornerus
evidence: The previous page names Cornerus as Vice-Chancellor, absent through illness, with the speaker acting in his place.

claim: Shao Yong was a Ming-dynasty philosopher who wrote the Huangji jingshi
evidence: Shao Yong (1011–1077) did write the Huangji jingshi, but he lived under the Northern Song, not the Ming.
correction: Northern Song dynasty (1011–1077), not Ming.

claim: Heading 'Commentary on Plato's Timaeus' (the work on this page)
evidence: BnF Grec 1841 contains Proclus' In Platonis Timaeum commentaria, books I–V, and the page names Timaeus. The heading is correct as an identification of the work, but it is not printed on the page.
correction: Correct as fact, but it is an editorial heading that is not in the source. Mark it as editorial or drop it.

claim: Meta: on this page Proclus applies the mathematical ratios to 'the immortality of the soul'
evidence: The OCR is heavily corrupted (many stray 'ᾗ'). The only basis is one word, ἀθανάτους ('immortals'), and the translation's own note reads that as 'likely the younger gods or the immortal part of the soul'. The page contains no argument about the soul's immortality.
correction: Remove, or hedge it as a reading of ἀθανάτους (perhaps the 'younger gods').

claim: This page continues the 'Singing of the Pitch-Pipes' (唱吕) tables
evidence: The previous page is headed 上聲調唱吕一之四, which the translation renders 'Singing of the Pitch-Pipes', and this page carries the same sound/tone (音/聲) grid. These are part of Shao Yong's 聲音唱和圖.

claim: 'Fenton, S. G.' expanded to 'Samuel G. Fenton'
evidence: The only 'Samuel G. Fenton' found is an early-20th-century antique dealer. Nothing ties a Samuel G. Fenton of Belfast to the Percy Society around 1842, and the source gives only 'S. G.'
correction: Keep 'S. G. Fenton'.

claim: Frederick William Fairholt (1814–1866), English engraver and antiquary who illustrated works on English history and costume
evidence: Wikipedia: English antiquary and wood-engraver, 1814–1866, author of Costume in England (1846).

claim: Barron Field (1786–1846), judge and poet, friend of Charles Lamb
evidence: Wikipedia: 23 Oct 1786 – 11 Apr 1846, poet and judge of the NSW Supreme Court, friend of Charles Lamb.

claim: William Stevenson Fitch (1793–1859), postmaster and collector of regional antiquities
evidence: Wikipedia/DNB: 1793–1859, postmaster of Ipswich for more than 21 years, collector of Suffolk antiquities.

claim: William Edward Forster (1818–1886), industrialist and politician, architect of the 1870 Education Act
evidence: Wikipedia: industrialist and Liberal MP for Bradford, 1818–1886, who steered the Elementary Education Act 1870 through Parliament.

claim: John Forster (1812–1876), biographer and critic, friend and biographer of Dickens
evidence: Wikipedia: 2 Apr 1812 – 2 Feb 1876, Dickens's friend and first biographer.

claim: F. J. Furnivall (1825–1910), co-creator of the Oxford English Dictionary and founder of the Early English Text Society
evidence: Wikipedia: one of the three founders and second editor of the OED, and founded the EETS in 1864.

claim: 'Gelty' is Edmund Getty
evidence: Edmund Getty was a Belfast antiquary, a fit for a Belfast member of an antiquarian text society; 'Gelty' is a plausible OCR or print slip.

claim: Edmund Getty (1799–1857), antiquary and secretary of the Belfast Harbour Commissioners
evidence: DIB: 1799–1857, antiquarian, appointed secretary to the Belfast harbour commissioners in 1847.

claim: John Graham-Gilbert (1794–1866), Scottish portrait painter
evidence: Wikipedia: Scottish portrait painter, 1794 – 4 June 1866.

claim: Sir Isaac Lyon Goldsmid (1778–1859), financier and first Jewish baronet in England
evidence: Wikipedia: 1778–1859, financier, created baronet in 1841, the first British Jew to receive a hereditary title.

claim: Lewis Dunbar Brodie Gordon (1815–1876), civil engineer and first Regius Professor of Civil Engineering and Mechanics in the UK
evidence: Univ. of Glasgow: 1815–1876, first Regius Professor of Civil Engineering and Mechanics and the first engineering professor appointed in the UK.

claim: Captain Charles Gray (1782–1851), Royal Marines officer and Scottish songwriter
evidence: Wikipedia/DNB: 1782–1851, captain in the Royal Marines and songwriter, who retired to Edinburgh.

claim: William Greenwell (1820–1918), archaeologist and Anglican clergyman known for barrow excavations
evidence: Wikipedia: 1820–1918, Canon of Durham, born at Greenwell Ford, excavated barrows.

claim: Tibetan 'bras bu gsum = Sanskrit triphala ('three fruits')
evidence: RYWiki: 'bras bu gsum = the three medicinal fruits (a ru ra, ba ru ra, skyu ru ra), i.e. triphala.

claim: Tibetan phung po = Sanskrit skandha (aggregates)
evidence: RYWiki: phung po = skandhas, aggregates, psycho-physical constituents.

claim: Tibetan dGa' ba'i sde = Sanskrit Harisena
evidence: Sanghata Sutra name appendix: 'Nandasena (Tibetan: dga' ba'i sde or dga' sde) — He Whose Army is Joy'.
correction: dga' ba'i sde renders Nandasena ('Joyful Army'), not Harisena (hari = tawny/Vishnu/lion, not joy).

claim: Dri med 'od zer (Drime Ozer) is Longchenpa
evidence: Longchen Rabjam Drimé Özer (1308–1364), or simply Longchenpa; Pema Lingpa regarded as his incarnation, fitting a prayer in the Pema Lingpa Kabum.

claim: Ban de Chos grub (Chödrub) is Facheng, a famous 9th-century translator
evidence: Chos grub (Chinese Facheng 法成) flourished early 9th c. at Dunhuang, translating Chinese texts into Tibetan; colophon here says 'translated from the Chinese manuscript'.

claim: Shariputra is the Buddha's disciple foremost in supernatural powers
evidence: Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom; Maudgalyāyana is foremost in supernatural (miraculous) powers.
correction: Shariputra is foremost in wisdom; Maudgalyayana is foremost in supernatural powers.

claim: 'Purana' is Purana Kashyapa, a non-Buddhist teacher
evidence: Pūraṇa Kassapa (Skt. Pūrṇa Kāśyapa) was one of the six non-Buddhist teachers contemporary with the Buddha; context contrasts a follower of Purana with a follower of the Buddha.

claim: Marpa's son is Dharma (Darma) Dode
evidence: Darma Dode was the son of Marpa Lotsawa and Dakmema; died young after a riding accident, transferring consciousness (powa).

claim: The unnamed retinue ('surrounded by ...') in this passage refers to Darma Dode or a deity
evidence: Marpa biographies attest Darma Dode as his son, but the elided passage (leaf-break, a group who 'came to welcome me' to the Sky-faring Realm) more plausibly refers to dakinis; no source fixes this identification.

claim: The 'unobstructed wheel' refers to the wheel of a chakravartin king
evidence: Cakraratna, the wheel jewel, is the first of the seven treasures of a universal monarch (cakravartin), whose wheel rolls everywhere without obstruction.

claim: Sanskrit title of the Bodhisattva Basket sutra is Ārya-bodhisattvapiṭaka-nāma-mahāyāna-sūtra
evidence: 84000 Toh 56 gives the Sanskrit title Āryabodhisatvapiṭakanāmamahāyānasūtra, 'The Noble Mahāyāna Sūtra The Collected Teachings on the Bodhisatva'.

claim: Śakra is the king of the gods, also known as Indra
evidence: 84000 glossary (brgya byin): Śakra, also known as Indra, is the lord of the gods in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.

claim: Dri med 'od zer is Longchenpa, a great Nyingma master
evidence: Treasury of Lives: Longchenpa Drime Wozer, one of the greatest philosophers and authors of the Nyingma tradition.

claim: Longchenpa was a 16th-century master
evidence: Treasury of Lives gives Longchenpa's dates as 1308-1364.
correction: Longchenpa (1308-1364) was a 14th-century master, not 16th-century.

claim: Tibetan Sha ra dwa ti'i bu = 'son of Śāradvatī', a name for Śāriputra
evidence: Wikipedia: to honor his mother he was named Śāradvatīputra, or in contracted form Śāriputra; 84000 glossary entity-40346 (ཤ་ར་དྭ་ཏིའི་བུ།) equates the Tibetan with Śāradvatīputra.

claim: Śāradvatīputra is the personal name of the disciple Śāriputra
evidence: Wikipedia: Śāriputra was born Upatiṣya; Śāradvatīputra is a matronymic ('son of Śāradvatī/Śārikā') honoring his mother.
correction: Śāradvatīputra does refer to Śāriputra, but it is a matronymic (son of Śāradvatī), not his personal name; his personal/birth name was Upatiṣya.

claim: Tibetan thog ma dang tha ma med pa stong pa nyid = Sanskrit anavarāgra-śūnyatā (emptiness of that which has no beginning or end)
evidence: Rigpa Wiki, Sixteen kinds of emptiness: thog ma dang mtha' ma med pa'i stong pa nyid, Skt. anavarāgraśūnyatā, emptiness of that which has no beginning nor end.

claim: Sanskrit Jinaputra ('sons of the Conqueror') is a title for bodhisattvas
evidence: 84000 glossary rgyal ba'i sras: Jinaputra, 'child of the jinas', an epithet for a bodhisattva; used frequently in The Ten Bhūmis.

claim: Rigdzin Chenpo ('Great Knowledge-Holder') here refers to Pema Lingpa
evidence: Pema Lingpa (1450-1521), Bhutanese tertön styled Rigdzin; founded his seat at Chokhor (Tamzhing) and died there in 1521, matching a Pad gling rnam thar passage about omens at Chokhor before his passing.

claim: The 'six teachers' are the non-Buddhist teachers contemporary with the Buddha
evidence: Wikipedia: the Six Heretical Teachers / Six Tirthikas were six sectarian contemporaries of Gautama Buddha, each holding views opposed to his teachings.

claim: The five heinous (anantarya) crimes are killing father, mother, or an arhat; wounding a Buddha; causing a schism in the Sangha
evidence: Wikipedia lists the five anantarika-karma as killing one's mother, father, an arahant, wounding a Tathagata, and creating division in the Sangha.

claim: 'Pang Lo' is the translator Pang Lotsawa Lodro Tenpa
evidence: Treasury of Lives: Pang Lotsawa Lodro Tenpa (1276-1342), a prominent scholar of Sanskrit grammar who wrote many expositions on Sanskrit grammar; fits a passage on Sanskrit letter-conjunction rules.

claim: The quoted verse is the Ye Dharma formula summarizing the Buddhist view of causality (dependent origination)
evidence: Wikipedia (Pratityasamutpada Gatha / Ye Dharma Hetu): the verse 'Those dharmas which arise from a cause, the Tathagata has declared their cause...' summarizes dependent origination.

claim: Jivaka was the famous doctor of the Buddha
evidence: Wikipedia: Jivaka Komarabhacca was the personal physician of the Buddha and King Bimbisara.

claim: Varshakara was a chief minister of Magadha
evidence: DPPN (palikanon.com): Vassakara was a brahmin and chief minister of Ajatasattu, king of Magadha.

claim: Tibetan mu stegs can = Sanskrit tirthika
evidence: 84000 glossary: tirthika, Tibetan mu stegs can, used for teachers of rival (non-Buddhist) religious traditions; matches 'non-Buddhists' in the passage.

claim: Tibetan sangs rgyas = Sanskrit Dharma
evidence: Search results (Encyclopedia of Buddhism / Sukhasiddhi / Wiktionary): sangs rgyas (Sangye) is the standard Tibetan translation of Sanskrit buddha; Dharma is chos.
correction: sangs rgyas = Sanskrit buddha ('homage to all the Buddhas'); Sanskrit dharma = Tibetan chos.

claim: Sharadvatiputra is a leading disciple of the Buddha, known for his wisdom (Shariputra)
evidence: Wikipedia: Shariputra, sometimes called Sharadvatiputra (son of Sharadvati), is considered the disciple foremost in wisdom.

claim: Tibetan bsod nams stobs = Sanskrit Punyabala (name of the prince 'Meritorious Power')
evidence: Rigpa Wiki: The Account of the Noble Deeds of Punyabala (Skt. Punyabalavadana, Toh 347) in which the Buddha was born as prince Punyabala; 84000 authority entity-24924 gives bsod nams stobs = 'Power of Merit'.

claim: Tushita is the heaven of the Thirty-Three gods, ruled by Indra
evidence: Trāyastriṃśa is 'the second of the six heavens of the desire realm' whose chief is Śakra/Indra; Wikipedia's Tushita article places Tushita between the Yāma and Nirmāṇarati heavens (the fourth heaven).
correction: Tushita is the fourth desire-realm heaven (between Yāma and Nirmāṇarati), not Trāyastriṃśa; the Heaven of the Thirty-Three ruled by Indra/Śakra is the second heaven.

claim: 'Dul ba rnam par 'byed pa = Sanskrit Vinaya-vibhanga
evidence: Toh 3 in the Kangyur is the Vinayavibhaṅga, Tibetan 'dul ba rnam par 'byed pa, 'The Detailed Exposition of the Vinaya' (84000 Discipline section).

claim: 'The Eight Thousand' refers to the Prajnaparamita Sutra in 8,000 (lines/verses)
evidence: The Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā (sher phyin brgyad stong pa), 'Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines', Toh 12; 'lines' is the standard rendering, 'verse' (śloka-units) is a loose but acceptable gloss.

claim: Sharadvatiputra is the son of Sharadvati, also known as Shariputra
evidence: His mother was named Śārī (alternatively Śāradvatī); he became known as Śāriputra and sometimes Śāradvatīputra (son of Śāradvatī).

claim: This is the 'Sealed Command of Auspiciousness' (bkra shis bka' rgya ma)
evidence: Khyung pos mdzad pa'i bkra shis bka' rgya ma, a Shangpa protector benediction 'essential for the establishment of the protector'; the passage is an auspiciousness verse in a six-armed Mahakala torma rite, consistent with this text.

claim: It was composed by the Great Siddha Drubchen Nyungpo
evidence: 'This benediction was composed by the Great Siddha Khyungpo' (Khyungpo Naljor, founder of the Shangpa Kagyu).
correction: The author is the Great Siddha Khyungpo (Khyungpo Naljor), not 'Nyungpo' — the name is garbled (and 'Great Siddha Drubchen' is redundant: drubchen = great siddha).

claim: Subhuti is a primary disciple of the Buddha known for his insight into emptiness
evidence: 'In Mahayana Buddhism, he is considered foremost in understanding emptiness'; one of the central figures in the Prajñāpāramitā sutras.

claim: Padmasambhava is the 8th-century Indian master who established Buddhism in Tibet
evidence: A tantric master 'from medieval India' (Oddiyana) who came to Tibet in the 8th century under Trisong Detsen and is credited with founding Samye and transmitting Vajrayana; 'established' simplifies a shared role with Śāntarakṣita and the king, but is the standard traditional attribution.

claim: 'Conflict-Free' ('thab bral) is the Yāma realm, the third heaven of the desire realm
evidence: 84000 glossary: 'thab bral, Heaven Free from Strife, Yāma, the third of the six heavens of the desire realm; named because its devas need not fight the asuras.

claim: Tibetan 'Jig rten 'dzin = Sanskrit Lokeshvara or Jagaddhara
evidence: 84000 glossary: 'jig rten 'dzin = Sanskrit Lokadhara (Chinese 持世), a bodhisattva and main interlocutor of The Inquiry of Lokadhara (Toh 174), a sutra on aggregates, elements and the twelve links.
correction: 'Jig rten 'dzin is Lokadhara. Lokeśvara is 'jig rten dbang phyug (a different figure, Avalokiteśvara); 'Jagaddhara' is not the attested equivalent. The passage (dependent origination addressed to 'World-Holder') matches the Lokadhara sutra.

claim: 'The lord' is Atisha, a Bengali master who came to Tibet in 1042 at the invitation of the kings of Guge
evidence: Born into a royal family in what is today Bangladesh ... invited to Tibet by the rulers of the Western Tibetan kingdom of Guge (Yeshe O and his nephew Jangchub O) ... He arrived in Tibet in 1042.

claim: Sharadvatiputra is Shariputra, the Buddha's disciple known for wisdom
evidence: Upatiṣya ... became known as Śāriputra (son of Śāri) and sometimes Śāradvatīputra (son of Śāradvatī); the Buddha declared him foremost in wisdom.

claim: Musulundha is a king or deity (equated with Mucilinda) acting as a teacher
evidence: 84000 Toh 287 glossary g.950: Musulundha (mu su lun dha) — 'King of the gods in the Heaven Free from Strife' (Yāma heaven); the text has him teach the Dharma to the gods. No equation with Mucilinda.
correction: Musulundha is the king of the gods of the Heaven Free from Strife (Yāma) in the Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna; he is not Mucilinda (the nāga king who sheltered the Buddha). 'King/deity acting as teacher' is right; the '/Mucilinda' equation is wrong.

claim: Upali is the Buddha's disciple specialized in monastic discipline
evidence: Upāli is described as 'foremost in monastic discipline'; 'In the literature of every Buddhist school, Upāli is depicted as an expert in vinaya.'

claim: Śāradvatīputra means son of Śāradvatī and is another name for Śāriputra
evidence: 84000 glossary g.1147 Śāradvatīputra (sha ra dwa ti'i bu): 'More widely known as Śāriputra—the contracted version of his name'; Wikipedia: 'Śāradvatīputra (son of Śāradvatī)'.

claim: Shakra is the king of gods, also addressed as Kaushika
evidence: 84000 glossary g.766 Kauśika: 'An epithet of the god Śakra, also known as Indra, the king of the gods in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.'

claim: Tibetan ming dang gzugs = Sanskrit nāmarūpa (name and form)
evidence: 84000 glossary (Toh 9; also Toh 211 g.19): 'name and form — Wylie: ming dang gzugs; Sanskrit: nāmarūpa; Fourth of the twelve links of dependent origination.'

claim: The Brahmin Sukhamahāsiddha is likely Garab Dorje's father
evidence: Garab Dorje's conception is miraculous (the nun Sudharmā dreams of a white man; tradition names the deity Adhicitta as father); no brahmin is named as his father.
correction: No source makes a brahmin Garab Dorje's father. In this Yangti lineage (Vajrasattva → the Brahmin → Śrī Siṃha) the brahmin holds the slot of a master before Śrī Siṃha (Garab Dorje/Mañjuśrīmitra position; the cycle is the 'Yang ti bram ze' Brahmin Cycle); the specific person could not be verified.

claim: The Brahmin Sukhamahāsiddha is a master in the Dzogchen lineage
evidence: Search snippet (page itself unreachable): the Yang ti bram ze ('Brahmin Cycle') was discovered by 'Brom Ye shes snying po, matching this colophon; the brahmin's own identity was not found in any fetched source. That he is a lineage master is evident from the passage itself.

claim: The 'Explanation of the Intent' is the Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra
evidence: 84000 Toh 106 'Unraveling the Intent' ('phags pa dgongs pa nges par 'grel pa, Saṃdhinirmocana), ch. 3 argues the faults that follow if the characteristics of conditioned phenomena and the ultimate were indistinct or distinct — exactly the cited argument.
